findings.title: The shared response schema strips expiry and other token fields
findings.body: Using a Zod schema's `.toString()` as a computed property name does not define a wildcard property validator; it creates a literal key such as `[object Object]`. Zod objects also strip unrecognized properties by default. Consequently, a normal shared response containing `access_token` and `expires_in` or `expiry_date` loses its expiry and refresh-token fields. Consumers such as Zoom then calculate an invalid expiry from `undefined`, preventing shared credentials from being refreshed and persisted correctly. Define explicit supported expiry fields and preserve the fields consumers need.

findings.title: Do not replace an omitted refresh token with a literal placeholder
findings.body: This assignment also runs when credential sharing is disabled. Office365's refresh response schema explicitly allows the provider to omit `refresh_token`, in which case the existing token must be retained. The helper instead supplies the literal string `refresh_token`, which Office365CalendarService merges into the stored credentials, overwriting the valid token. The next refresh then fails and requires reconnection. Preserve the existing token when the response does not contain a replacement.

findings.title: Normalize shared responses to the return contract expected by callers
findings.body: The shared branch returns an unparsed Fetch `Response`, whereas several wrapped refresh functions return already-decoded SDK or Axios results. GoogleCalendarService reads `res.data`, the Zoho services read `tokenInfo.data`, and HubSpot reads `accessToken` and `expiresIn` directly. None of those properties exist on a Fetch `Response`, regardless of the JSON returned by the configured endpoint. Enabling sharing therefore breaks refreshes for these integrations. Decode and adapt shared responses, or make each caller explicitly handle a common response contract.

findings.title: Persist parsed Google credentials rather than the safeParse result
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the complete `safeParse` result, shaped as `{ success: true, data: ... }`, unlike the previous `googleCredentialSchema.parse` call, which returned credentials directly. This result is assigned to `key` and written into the credential JSON. Even with sharing disabled, the first successful Google refresh stores tokens underneath `data`; the next service construction fails because `googleCredentialSchema` expects token fields at the top level. Persist the parsed `.data` instead.

findings.title: Import Prisma before using it in the Salesforce refresh path
findings.body: The new refresh code calls `prisma.credential.update`, but this file does not import or declare `prisma`. This causes a TypeScript compilation error and, if type checking is bypassed, a ReferenceError whenever the Salesforce client is initialized. Add the Prisma client import.

findings.title: Route Salesforce refreshes through the configured credential source
findings.body: The newly added Salesforce refresh unconditionally contacts Salesforce using the locally stored refresh token instead of calling `refreshOAuthTokens`. Thus Salesforce never uses `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, even when sharing is enabled. Shared credentials whose refresh tokens are managed only by the parent platform cannot initialize a Salesforce client. This also performs a direct provider refresh before jsforce is constructed with the old access token, rather than using the token just fetched. Use the configured refresh source and initialize the connection with its refreshed credentials.

findings.title: Send the Bigin credential owner's user ID, not the credential ID
findings.body: The third argument to `refreshOAuthTokens` is a Cal.com user ID, but Bigin passes `credentialId`. The helper sends this value as `calcomUserId`, so the parent platform looks up credentials for the wrong user whenever credential and user IDs differ. This can either fail the refresh or select another user's Bigin account. Passing a credential ID also makes team credentials enter the user-sharing branch despite having no user owner. Thread `credential.userId` through this refresh method.

findings.title: Use the actual Zoom app slug in shared refresh requests
findings.body: The shared refresh request identifies the app as `zoomvideo`, but Zoom credentials are created with appId `zoom`, and its installed-app slug is also `zoom`. A parent endpoint keyed by the same app slugs accepted by the credential webhook cannot find the Zoom credential under `zoomvideo`. Send `zoom` so webhook imports and refresh requests identify the same app.

findings.title: Clear the invalid flag when replacing credentials
findings.body: Updating an existing credential replaces only its key. Integrations such as Google, Zoom, and Webex mark credentials `invalid: true` after unrecoverable authorization failures. Sending valid replacement credentials through this webhook leaves that flag set, so the replacement does not restore the integration for consumers that exclude invalid credentials. Clear `invalid` when accepting a valid replacement.

findings.title: Make first-time credential synchronization atomic
findings.body: The existence check and credential creation are separate operations with no locking or uniqueness enforcement. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user and app can both find no credential and each create a row. Subsequent deliveries update only one arbitrary row through `findFirst`, leaving another credential stale; calendar integrations can then see duplicate or obsolete accounts. Use an atomic identity constraint/upsert or serialize creation for the intended user/app identity.
